site.name: HK Traffic Sign Map

about.h1: About the HK Traffic Sign Map
about.whatP2: It starts from the questions a driver brings: where can I drive, stop or pick up? The road-rules layer draws where each rule actually applies — speed-limit stretches, bus-only lanes with their hours, vehicle prohibitions, no-stopping restrictions and pedestrian zones — along with the roads public light buses cannot reach at all because every way in is closed to them, and which of Hong Kong’s three taxi colours may serve a given street.
about.whatP3: Underneath, every sign in the Transport Department’s open dataset sits on one fast, zoomable map, so you can see exactly which signs stand on any street — useful for drivers and learner drivers, road-safety and town-planning research, accessibility audits, or simple curiosity.
about.how1: Pan and zoom to any street; signs spread apart as you zoom in.
about.how2: The panel opens on the Road rules tab: turn on a row to draw where that rule applies and narrow the map to the signs that announce it, and use “Show all signs” to bring the rest back. Click a line for its details; “Show signs for this rule” narrows the map to that one rule’s signs.
about.how3: Click a sign or dot to inspect it. Click the same spot again to cycle through several overlapping signs.
about.how4: In the Signs tab, toggle sign classes on or off, or switch to “By sign ID” to search for particular signs by number or meaning; a matched sign brings the rest of its signpost with it. Fold the panel away for a larger map.
about.how5: Each plate is turned the way it faces on the street and drawn as if laid flat on the ground, so it reads upright from the side its drivers approach. Signs sharing a post hang together in one column.

about.disclaimer: This is an independent, informational project. It is not affiliated with the Transport Department and must not be relied on for navigation or as a legal authority on road traffic regulations. Some readings — the roads minibuses cannot reach, taxi operating areas and expressways — are worked out or curated here rather than published by the department, and any of the data can lag behind changes on the road. Drivers should always follow the signs and markings on the road and check the department’s latest {notices} and road conditions. faq.metaDescription: Frequently asked questions and a quick user guide for the HK Traffic Sign Map: the road-rules layer (speed limits, no stopping, minibus no-go roads, taxi areas), how to read and filter signs, data sources, how current the data is, and mobile use.

items.q: What is the HK Traffic Sign Map?
items.a: It is a free, interactive web map of Hong Kong’s road rules and traffic signs. It draws where speed limits, no-stopping restrictions, bus lanes and vehicle bans apply, which roads minibuses cannot reach and where each taxi colour may serve, and shows every installed sign: catalogued signs as their real pictogram, everything else as a colour-coded dot you can click to inspect.

items.q: Where does the sign data come from?
items.a: From the Hong Kong Transport Department’s open datasets on data.gov.hk: “Traffic Aids Drawings (2nd generation)” for the signs, and “Road Network (2nd generation)” for the road rules and the direction each sign faces. Chinese sign names come from the department’s Road Users’ Code. The basemap is © OpenStreetMap contributors.

The Transport Department refreshes the source dataset roughly monthly. This site is rebuilt from that data, so it reflects the most recent published release rather than live, real-time changes. Each road-rule popup says how old its reading is: the day the road network data was fetched, or, for taxi areas and expressways, the date of the legal source they were checked against.

items.q: How do I find and inspect a sign?
items.a: Zoom into any street. Signs spread apart as you zoom in. Click a sign or dot to open its details; if several signs overlap, click again on the same spot to cycle through each one.

items.q: What do the colours and categories mean?
items.a: Signs are grouped into their Index-Plan classes — Regulatory, Warning, Informatory, Supplementary and Temporary — plus Tourist and uncatalogued Other signs. Each class has its own colour in the legend and can be toggled on or off independently.

items.q: Why do some signs show as a coloured dot instead of a picture?
items.a: A sign is drawn as its real pictogram once you zoom in past its level-of-detail threshold and if it exists in the pictogram catalogue. Until then, or for not-yet-catalogued signs, it stays a coloured dot so it is never hidden.

items.q: Which way do the signs face?
items.a: Each sign is turned to the direction it faces, worked out from the direction of travel on the road beside its pole, and drawn as if laid flat on the ground — so it reads upright from the side the drivers it addresses approach. Signs on the same post hang in one column; a pole with signs on both sides shows a column for each side. No published source records which way a sign faces, so treat the facing as an estimate, especially at junctions.

items.q: Can I filter which signs are shown?
items.a: Yes. The Signs tab toggles any sign class on or off, or hides them all at once, and its “By sign ID” switch searches signs by number or meaning and shows only the ones you pick, each with the rest of its signpost. The panel can be folded away to give the map more room.

items.q: What are the coloured lines on the roads?
items.a: The Road rules tab, which the panel opens on, draws where a rule applies, straight from the Transport Department’s road network data: speed limits, bus-only lanes, vehicle prohibitions, no-stopping restrictions and pedestrian zones. Click a line for its details, including hours and days, and use “Show signs for this rule” to see the signs that announce it. The default 50 km/h limit has no line of its own.

Roads that public light buses may not use. Dashed lines are the routes the Transport Department prohibits them from; the wider shaded band marks roads that are cut off because every way in is closed by those prohibitions or by turn bans. The cut-off band is worked out by this site from the department’s own rules rather than published by it. Green minibuses running under route permits are not covered.

items.q: Which taxi colour can serve a street?
items.a: Turn on the taxi row and pick a colour with its chips. Green New Territories taxis get their permitted operating area, the designated routes the Transport Department draws on its boundary map — the thirteen it numbers and the unnumbered links that join them — and the fringe facilities they may serve: the airport, Disneyland, the Shenzhen Bay port, several stations, two hospitals and Sha Tin Racecourse. Blue Lantau taxis get Lantau and Chek Lap Kok. Red urban taxis serve almost everywhere, so that chip draws only the exception: Tung Chung Road and the roads of South Lantau. Unlike every other row, this one is not read off the road network data — no such dataset exists — so it is compiled here from Schedule 7 to Cap. 374E, which lists the permitted roads street by street, and each line says so when you click it. Where the Schedule permits only the stretch of a road between two junctions, the line stops at those junctions; a taxi rank inside a station’s transport interchange is not drawn, because the Schedule lists roads, not interchanges.

items.q: Does it work on a phone?
items.a: Yes. The map is responsive, supports touch pan/zoom, and can centre on your location if you grant location permission.

items.q: Is this an official government website?
items.a: No. It is an independent, informational project that visualises public open data. It is not affiliated with the Transport Department and must not be used for navigation or as a legal authority on road traffic regulations. Some readings are worked out here rather than published by the department, and the data can lag behind changes on the road, so drivers should always follow the signs on the road and check the Transport Department’s latest traffic notices. It is provided “as is”, with no warranty that it is accurate or up to date, and the author accepts no liability for any consequence of relying on it.
Yes, it is free. The underlying sign data is provided under the data.gov.hk Terms and Conditions; the basemap is OpenStreetMap.
